questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct tax?
options: Corporation tax
Value added tax
Excise duty on fuel
An import tariff
questions.why: Direct taxes are levied on income, profit or wealth; indirect taxes on spending.
whyNot: VAT is levied on spending.
Excise duty is levied on spending.
A tariff is levied on spending on imports.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a regressive tax?
options: A tax that takes a falling proportion of income as income rises
A tax that takes a rising proportion of income as income rises
A tax that takes the same proportion at all income levels
A tax that falls only on the wealthy
questions.why: Indirect taxes are generally regressive, because the poorest spend a larger proportion of their income.
whyNot: That is a progressive tax.
That is a proportional tax.
That would be progressive in the extreme.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the marginal tax rate?
options: The proportion of an additional unit of income paid in tax
Total tax paid as a proportion of total income
The highest rate in the tax schedule
The rate paid by the average taxpayer
questions.why: The marginal rate determines the incentive effect; the average rate determines the burden.
whyNot: That is the average tax rate.
The marginal rate for an individual depends on their income, not the top band.
That is closer to the average rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following distinguishes tax avoidance from tax evasion?
options: Avoidance is lawful; evasion is not
Avoidance applies to firms; evasion to individuals
Avoidance applies to direct taxes; evasion to indirect taxes
They are the same thing
questions.why: Both reduce revenue, and only one is a criminal matter.
whyNot: Both can be done by either.
Both can apply to either type of tax.
The legal status differs.

questions.stem: An allowance of $10,000, then 20% up to $40,000, then 40% above. What tax does someone on $25,000 pay?
whyNot: That applies 20% to the whole income.
That applies too high a rate.
That uses an incorrect taxable income.

questions.stem: Using the same schedule, what tax does someone on $80,000 pay?
whyNot: That applies 40% to the whole taxable income.
That applies 40% to the whole income.
That omits the 20% band.

questions.stem: Tax of $3,000 on $25,000 and $22,000 on $80,000. What kind of tax is this?
options: Progressive, because the average rate rises from 12% to 27.5%
Regressive, because the higher earner pays more in total
Proportional, because both pay tax
Regressive, because the marginal rate is 40%
questions.why: A tax is progressive when it takes a rising proportion of income, not merely a rising amount.
whyNot: Paying more in total is not the test; the proportion is.
The proportions differ, so it is not proportional.
A high top marginal rate is a feature of a progressive tax.

questions.stem: A 15% sales tax. A spends all of $25,000; B spends $50,000 of $80,000. What does this show?
options: The tax is regressive: A pays 15% of income and B pays 9.4%
The tax is progressive: B pays more in total
The tax is proportional: both pay 15% of spending
The tax has no distributional effect
questions.why: A pays $3,750 on $25,000 of income; B pays $7,500 on $80,000. The poorest spend a larger proportion of income, so they pay a larger proportion in tax.
whyNot: Paying more in total does not make it progressive.
As a share of income, which is what matters, the rates differ.
The effect is clearly regressive.

questions.stem: Why can a cut in income tax fail to raise the hours people work?
options: The income effect may dominate: higher income for the same hours can encourage more leisure
Nobody responds to financial incentives
Tax cuts always reduce disposable income
Hours worked are fixed by law
questions.why: The substitution and income effects pull in opposite directions, and for higher earners the income effect can dominate.
whyNot: Many people do respond; the direction is the question.
A tax cut raises disposable income.
Some hours are contractual, not legally fixed.

questions.stem: What does the Laffer curve show?
options: Tax revenue rising as the rate rises up to a point, then falling
Tax revenue rising continuously with the tax rate
Tax revenue falling continuously with the tax rate
The relationship between tax rates and inflation
questions.why: At 0% revenue is zero, and at 100% it is also zero because nobody works for nothing, so there is a revenue-maximising rate.
whyNot: Beyond the maximising rate, revenue falls.
Revenue rises initially.
It concerns revenue, not inflation.

questions.stem: The current tax rate is below the revenue-maximising rate. What happens if it is cut?
options: Revenue falls
Revenue rises
Revenue is unchanged
Revenue rises then falls
questions.why: Cutting a rate only raises revenue if the rate is above t*, and in most countries most of the time it is below.
whyNot: That would be the case only if the rate were above t*.
A rate change moves revenue unless at the peak.
A single cut produces a single movement.

questions.stem: Why is the Laffer argument stronger for corporation tax than for income tax on employees?
options: The revenue-maximising rate is much lower for mobile tax bases than for workers who cannot relocate
Corporation tax raises more revenue
Companies are legally exempt from income tax
Employees never respond to tax rates
questions.why: Corporate profit can be shifted between jurisdictions; the wages of ordinary employees cannot.
whyNot: Income tax usually raises far more.
Companies pay corporation tax on profit; the comparison is about mobility.
They respond somewhat, though far less than mobile capital.

questions.stem: Why can the effective marginal rate at the bottom of the income distribution exceed that at the top?
options: Benefit withdrawal combines with income tax to produce a very high combined rate
The poorest pay a higher statutory rate
Indirect taxes are levied only on low earners
The tax-free allowance does not apply to low earners
questions.why: That is the poverty trap, and it means the weakest work incentives in the economy can be at the bottom.
whyNot: Statutory rates are lower at the bottom.
Indirect taxes apply to everyone.
The allowance applies to all taxpayers.

questions.stem: Why can the distributional effect of a tax not be judged from the tax alone?
options: It depends on what the revenue funds, so a regressive tax funding services used by the poorest can be redistributive overall
Tax incidence cannot be measured
All taxes are equally distributed in their effect
Spending has no distributional effect
questions.why: Judging a tax in isolation from the spending it funds is a common and serious error.
whyNot: Incidence is studied extensively.
Their incidence differs sharply.
Spending is strongly redistributive in most systems.

questions.stem: Why do developing countries rely more on indirect taxes?
options: Collecting income tax requires records, formal employment and administrative capacity
Indirect taxes are more progressive
Income tax is prohibited by the IMF
Indirect taxes raise more revenue in every country
questions.why: The consequence is that the tax system tends to be less progressive, not by preference but because of capacity.
whyNot: Indirect taxes are generally regressive.
No such prohibition exists.
Direct taxes dominate in most developed economies.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a rise in an indirect tax on the price level?
options: A one-off increase in the price level, rather than continuing inflation unless wages respond
Continuing inflation indefinitely
No effect, because it falls on producers
A fall in the price level
questions.why: It raises prices directly, and the effect is a level shift rather than a sustained rate of increase.
whyNot: A single tax change does not sustain inflation by itself.
It is passed on to consumers in the price.
It raises prices.
